opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, failure was a much bigger part of the story than the honors were. When people look back, they see the medals or the recognition and assume it was a smooth line upward. It really wasn't. Most of the time spent on Olympiad math is time spent being stuck. You sit with a problem for hours, sometimes days, and you don't solve it. That's the normal state.

So early on I had to change how I related to failing. At first, not solving a problem felt like a verdict on me: maybe I'm just not smart enough, maybe other people see things I can't. Over time I realized that the failed attempts are where the learning actually happens. When you finally read a solution after struggling for a long time, you understand *why* your approaches didn't work, and that sticks with you in a way that just reading the answer never does. The struggle is the training.

Competitions themselves were also humbling. There were contests where I didn't do as well as I hoped, where one problem went wrong and that was it. That hurts, especially when you're young and you've invested so much. But I think those moments taught me something about resilience that turned out to matter far beyond math. You learn to separate your self-worth from a single result. You learn to go back, look honestly at what happened, and keep going.

And I think that mindset carried into research and later into building things. In research, almost everything you try fails. If you haven't made peace with that, you can't survive it. Olympiads were kind of my first practice ground for being comfortable with not knowing, and for treating failure as information rather than as a final judgment.

r001.rationale: The response describes Olympiad work as repeatedly being stuck and struggling, then calls it her first practice ground for becoming comfortable with not knowing—presenting that ongoing challenge as formative.

r002.rationale: It says most Olympiad time is spent being stuck and that not solving problems is the normal state, clearly framing failure as the default.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When people hear "Olympiad gold medal," they tend to picture a straight line, but for me the line was anything but straight, and I think failure was actually the most important part of it.

I'll be honest: for a long time I wasn't winning. I remember sitting through competitions where I'd stare at a problem for three hours and come away with nothing, not even a partial idea. In the early years I was often not selected, or I'd make a team and then perform below what I knew I was capable of. Those moments stung. There's a very specific kind of loneliness in competitive math, because the result is so unambiguous. The problem either got solved or it didn't. You can't talk your way around a blank page.

What changed for me was how I understood what those failures were telling me. At first I read them as a verdict on my ability. Over time I started reading them as information. If I couldn't solve a geometry problem, that wasn't the universe telling me I wasn't a mathematician. It was telling me exactly which tool I was missing. So a failed problem became a to-do item rather than a judgment. I'd go back, figure out what the key idea was, and ask why I didn't see it. Usually there was a concrete, learnable reason.

The other thing failure taught me was patience with my own thinking. Olympiad problems are designed so that the obvious approach doesn't work. That means you are supposed to fail several times inside a single problem before you find the way through. Once I accepted that, the small failures stopped feeling like failures. They became part of the process, almost a rhythm. Try something, watch it break, learn why it broke, try again. That rhythm is really what mathematics is, at any level.

And I think the most valuable thing was emotional rather than technical. Competing taught me that I could feel genuinely terrible after a result, go home, and still show up the next morning to do more problems. That resilience turned out to matter far more than any particular lemma I memorized. When I later did research, when I started a company, the problems were different but the feeling was identical: most of what you try doesn't work, and the people who get somewhere are simply the ones who keep going with curiosity intact.

So if I'm being candid, I don't think I understood failure as a role I had chosen for it. It was more that failure was unavoidable, and I eventually learned to treat it as a teacher instead of an enemy. The medals were nice, but that shift in mindset is what I actually took with me.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated failures as formative, but does not communicate that continually being outside her comfort zone was formative.

r002.rationale: It presents failure as routine and unavoidable in her Olympiad pursuit, describing years without wins and repeated unsuccessful attempts as part of the process.

astra-6.text:
I see failure as part of learning mathematics. When I can’t solve a problem, it gives me something specific to examine: Was there a concept I didn’t understand? Did I commit to an approach too quickly? Or did I just need more time to explore?

Of course, that doesn’t mean disappointment feels good, especially when you’ve worked hard toward a competition. But I think it helps to separate a result from your ability to grow. Honors are meaningful, but the deeper value is learning to stay curious and keep thinking when the answer isn’t obvious.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from unsolved problems and staying curious, but does not say that continually being outside her comfort zone was formative.

r002.rationale: It calls failure part of learning, but does not characterize failure as the default in her pursuit of Olympiad honors.

sol-6.1.text:
I see failure as part of learning mathematics. When I can’t solve a problem, it exposes something I don’t yet understand—maybe a gap in my knowledge, or an assumption I haven’t questioned. The useful step is to go back and ask where my approach stopped working and what I could try differently.

Of course, it can be disappointing when you’ve worked hard and the result doesn’t reflect that. But Olympiad honors are an outcome; the understanding you build along the way stays with you. I think learning to be patient with being stuck is one of the most valuable parts of the experience.

r001.rationale: The response says failure helps reveal gaps and build understanding, but does not describe continually being outside her comfort zone as formative.
